vignette:
She is 63, an African woman who speaks about her life in careful, measured pieces, as if she has spent years learning how to keep the worst parts contained. Before she came to the United States, she lived in a country where the ground beneath ordinary life shifted too quickly to trust. She had worked hard, studied numbers, and built a career that relied on precision and calm judgment. As a financial analyst, she was known for being steady and exacting, someone who could track risk before others saw it coming. That habit of anticipating trouble, once a professional strength, becomes a way of surviving as violence spreads around her community.

When the conflict reaches her neighborhood, she does not leave all at once. Like many people forced into becoming refugees, she tries first to adapt, to wait, to tell herself that the danger will pass if she keeps her head down and stays useful. She remembers counting cash in dim light, hearing distant shouting, and trying to finish work while everyone around her speaks in urgent, lowered voices. The day she finally flees is not dramatic in the way movies portray escape. It is chaotic, humiliating, and full of interruptions. She leaves with too few belongings and no certainty that she will ever return. The loss that stays with her most is not only the danger itself but the collapse of the life she had made with such discipline. She grieves her home, her colleagues, her routines, and the version of herself who once moved through the world with confidence.

Even years later, she still organizes her days as if order might protect her. She arrives early to work, keeps her desk neat, and double-checks figures long after others would consider the task complete. Her competence is still there, but it is shadowed by vigilance. She watches entrances automatically, sits where she can see the room, and is unsettled by sudden voices or the slam of a door. She says that her body often reacts before her mind does: her heart speeds up, her shoulders tighten, and her stomach knots when she hears sirens, helicopters, or raised arguments in the street. At home, she leaves lights on longer than she needs to and checks locks more than once. She is single and lives alone, and although she values her independence, she also feels the emptiness of it at night, when the silence becomes too large and her thoughts begin to circle back to what was lost.

Sleep does not come easily. When she does fall asleep, it is shallow and interrupted by dreams that are not always exact replicas of the past but carry its fear with brutal clarity. She wakes disoriented, sometimes already crying, with the sense that she has been running. In the morning she feels exhausted, as if the night has taken something from her. Certain smells, sounds, and snippets of news can pull her back into the past without warning. She does not call them flashbacks in the abstract; she describes them as moments when she is suddenly there again, when the refugee camps, checkpoints, and panic rise up so vividly that her chest closes and she has to sit down. During those moments, she feels embarrassed by how quickly she can become overwhelmed, though she works hard to hide it from others.

She has learned to avoid too much exposure to conflict stories, because they come too close to her own history. She changes the channel when images of war appear and stops conversations that turn toward politics in the region she left behind. Even so, she finds herself thinking about the people who did not make it out, and about the choices she had no real power to make. There is a persistent sadness in her, mixed with guilt that she survived when so many others suffered. At times, she wonders whether she should have done more, stayed longer, or somehow protected others. These thoughts do not arrive neatly; they intrude during work, while shopping, or while sitting alone at dinner. She remains capable and active, but everything seems to take more effort than it once did.

What stands out most is how much of her life is now built around preventing a return of terror. She is disciplined, alert, and self-contained, yet beneath that composure lives a woman who has endured displacement, loss, and the long afterlife of danger.
